nameStory: The onion-stalk parasol gets its charming name from the distinctive bulbous swelling at the base of its stem, which looks remarkably like the bottom of a green onion or scallion. Just like how an onion bulb stores nutrients underground, this mushroom's swollen stem base helps anchor it in loose wood debris and mulch.
description: The onion-stalk parasol is a delicate, pale mushroom that pops up in wood chips, mulch, and sometimes potted plants throughout New England. It features a bell-shaped cap covered in fine scales and sits atop a slender stem with that telltale bulbous base. This elegant little fungus typically reaches 2-4 inches tall with caps about 1-3 inches across, making it a modest but distinctive find in gardens and landscaped areas.

idTips.label: Stem Base
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic bulbous swelling at the very bottom of the stem - it feels firm and rounded like a small onion bulb, often partially buried in the substrate

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Bell-shaped cap covered in fine, powdery scales that feel slightly rough to the touch; typically pale white to cream colored with a smooth margin

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Handle gently and watch for yellow to brownish staining where touched - this color change happens within minutes of handling

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: White gills that are free from the stem (don't attach to it) and feel delicate, almost papery when fresh

idTips.label: Partial Veil
idTips.description: Young specimens often show a thin ring or ring remnants on the upper stem from a partial veil that protected the developing gills

habitat: You'll find onion-stalk parasols thriving in wood chip mulch, decorative bark mulch, and compost-rich garden beds throughout New England. They're particularly common in landscaped areas around homes, parks, and botanical gardens where fresh wood debris provides their preferred growing medium. Occasionally they'll surprise you by appearing in large potted plants or greenhouse environments where wood-based potting mixes are used.

seasonality.spring: Early season fruiting begins as soil warms, especially after spring rains saturate wood chip mulch beds. Look for the first flushes in well-mulched garden areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for onion-stalk parasols, with regular flushes appearing 1-3 days after summer thunderstorms in wood chip mulch. Hot, humid conditions followed by rain trigger the most abundant fruiting.
seasonality.fall: Continued fruiting through early fall, particularly in October when autumn rains keep mulch beds consistently moist. Often the last mushrooms to appear before winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent during New England winters, existing only as dormant mycelium within wood debris, waiting for spring warmth and moisture to return.

funFact: This mushroom is essentially a tropical traveler that's become a New England garden resident - it likely arrived in our region hidden within commercial mulch and wood chips shipped from warmer climates, then adapted to our seasonal growing conditions!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small white parasol mushrooms, but that distinctive onion-bulb stem base is your foolproof identifier - no other common New England mushroom has quite the same bulbous stem bottom. Memory trick: 'Onion base = onion-stalk parasol!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'parasol,' this mushroom doesn't actually spread out like an umbrella - it maintains its bell shape throughout its life. The 'parasol' name comes from the broader mushroom family it belongs to, many of which do open into classic parasol shapes.
compareHints: Among its Leucocoprinus relatives, the onion-stalk parasol is distinguished by that unmistakable bulbous stem base - the flowerpot parasol is bright yellow, while other white dapperlings lack the pronounced stem swelling. The yellow-to-brown bruising reaction when handled also sets it apart from similar pale mushrooms in the same genus, which may not bruise or bruise different colors.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Leucocoprinus relatives, the flowerpot parasol stands out for its consistently bright yellow color and potted plant habitat.
Unlike its bright yellow cousin the Flowerpot Parasol, the White Dapperling stays consistently white throughout its development.
